rows.title: No eyes
rows.text: If you are the coral Acropora millepora, you carry blue-light cryptochromes, and the activity of your gene cry2 rises on full-moon nights compared with new-moon nights. Nobody has measured whether the coral Cycloseris cyclolites or the starlet anemone sense light in this way.
rows.note: No record states that these animals lack eyes, so I left "You have no eyes" out. The record also gives no function for cry2, so I made no claim about spawning.

rows.title: Full moon
rows.text: If you are a staghorn coral of the species Acropora millepora, your cells make a blue-light sensing protein called cryptochrome, and the amount of one kind, cry2, rises on full-moon nights compared with new-moon nights. Nobody has measured this in Cycloseris cyclolites, a mushroom coral, so nobody knows whether you sense moonlight the same way.
rows.note: R1 does not say the cells sense the moon directly or that cry2 drives spawning; the row states only the expression change. Common names for the two species are not in the records, so "staghorn coral" and "mushroom coral" may need checking.

rows.title: The dark hour
rows.text: If you are the coral Acropora millepora, you have no eyes, yet your cells make a blue-light sensing protein called cryptochrome. The gene for one kind, cry2, switches on more on full-moon nights than on new-moon nights, so your body can tell a bright night from a dark one. Nobody has measured this in Cycloseris cyclolites, a mushroom coral.
rows.note: R1 measures gene expression only; the quote does not say the coral's spawning depends on it, so the row stops short of that. Cycloseris is described as unmeasured, with no claim about its biology.

rows.title: Shadows
rows.text: When a shadow falls over you, a nerve of yours fires a long burst. If you are an Atlantic surf clam, each of your pallial nerves has one light-sensitive fiber that goes silent in the light. When the light stops, that fiber sends a prolonged burst of impulses at high frequency.
rows.note: R1 gives no firing rate, so I left out any number.

rows.title: Moon jellies
rows.text: If you are an Asian moon jellyfish, you pulse faster in light, and you spend more time in the lit side of a tank than in the dark side. That was measured in juveniles. Nobody has measured this in the greater moon jellyfish or the moon jellyfish, so for you the question is still open.
rows.note: Only R1 (Aurelia coerulea juveniles) supports a claim; no records for A. labiata or A. aurita, so they are stated as unmeasured.

rows.title: Scallops and giant clams
rows.text: If you are a bay scallop, your eyes can separate two details only when they are about 2 degrees apart, the width of a human thumb held at arm's length. If you are a small giant clam, you pull in your mantle when a dark spot is about 13 degrees wide, which is more than six thumbs side by side, and a spot a little under 12 degrees does not make you pull in.
rows.note: Left out king scallop: R3's quote is a table line that does not state the 0.314 value, so no figure is given for it.

rows.title: Box jellyfish
rows.text: If you are a mangrove box jellyfish, you avoid obstacles by sight, and you turn away once an obstacle fills a certain angle of what you see. If you are a herpes jelly, you hunt at night by swimming toward areas where your prey sets off flashes of its own light.
rows.note: R1 says only "avoidance"; I wrote "turn away" loosely. The record gives no figure for the angle, so none is stated.

rows.title: Eyes at the arm tips
rows.text: If you are a Pacific crown-of-thorns, the tiny units that make up each of your eyes point about 8 degrees apart. If you are a blue Linckia, they point about 16 degrees apart, which is twice as coarse. Juvenile Acanthaster measured about 17 degrees, and nobody has measured this in the purple starfish, the chocolate chip sea star or the Northern Pacific seastar.
rows.note: No record states that the eyes sit at the arm tips, so the row leaves that to the title. Removed the word "reports" and the review credit, since R1 and R2 are not marked PARTIAL.

rows.title: Gray and slow
rows.text: A crown-of-thorns starfish, a different sea star, stops seeing a light as flickering once it flashes faster than about once every two seconds, where a human stops at about 60 flashes a second. A review of the literature gives this as the slowest flicker limit measured in any animal eye. Nobody has measured how fast a flicker you can see.
rows.note: Flicker figure belongs to the crown-of-thorns starfish (Acanthaster) only, from a review. No record on color, so "gray" in the title is not claimed in the text.

failed.title: Sea urchins
failed.last: A human thumb held at arm's length covers about 2 degrees, and you need a target several thumbs wide before you can pick it out. If you are an Atlantic purple sea urchin, you turned toward targets only when they were 45 degrees wide or more, and if you are a Diadema africanum, you move toward dark objects only when they are 30 to 70 degrees wide, according to a modeling paper that draws on the behavioral test. If you are a Pacific purple sea urchin, the spacing of your spines predicts a finest detail of about 8 to 11 degrees, and if you are an Arctic green sea urchin, you very likely see about as coarsely as that close relative.
